Anatomy of Hope

By: Diana Lucas | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
Anatomy of Hope is surgeon Jerome Groopman’s best seller on how people prevail in the face of illness and how hope can radically alter the out come.

Why do some people find and sustain hope during difficult circumstances, while others do not? What can we learn from those who do and how is their example applicable to our own lives. His book Anatomy of Hope spans some thirty years of Groopman’s practice. Through encounters with many extraordinary people he sought to answer these questions. Using his background of science and the human factor Jerome explains how he distinguishes true hope from false and how this can essentially change or alter your diagnosis.

Reach for a dream have been going for 30 years and decided on their 30th Birthday that they would bring out Jerome Groopman M.D precisely because his his book and it’s message is their own vision. We have been promised an exclusive interview…together with that we will weave case studies of two families whose children’s wishes and hopes have been granted by Reach for A Dream.

Case Study 1 Lesedi Sekgolo is 16 years old and has been diagnosed with Ewings Sarcoma, a rare and difficult cancer that occurs around the bones. Lesedi loves to cook and her dream was to meet television personality Chef Siba.

Case Study 2 Arabella van Rooyen is 6 years old and has Nephroblastoma cancer of the kidneys that typically occurs in children. Arabella’s dream was to have her own drum set..

These are not huge wishes to fulfil but what does it give to the patient when these dreams are fulfilled, what sort positivity or hope sets in that could play a part in a more positive out come for their future.

Press Release:


An Anatomy of Hope
Lesedi Sekgolo is 16 years old and has Ewing’s Sarcoma, a rare cancer that affects the bones, while Arabella van Rooyen is just six years old with Nephroblastoma, a cancer of the kidneys. Yet these young children remain hopeful despite the challenging odds. So why do some people find and sustain hope during difficult circumstances, while others do not? Now after years of studying the recovery of his patients, US oncologist Dr Jerome Groopman, may finally have unlocked the answers.


Script:


Jerome Groopman: Hope is a very central and powerful aspect in medicine and yet it is something that unfortunately physicians like myself and other medical professionals don’t really think about or focus on.

Link Hope…. the Mind and Body’s relationship…. are not usually words we connect with the field of medical science but Dr. Jerome Groopman set out to research the vital role hope plays in the lives of patients suffering from severe illness’s. His Book Anatomy of Hope is the result

V/O 14 and half sec
Dr Groopman is one world’s leading researchers in cancer and aids and Professor of Medicine at Harvard. But when he started out thirty years ago the very idea of “hope” was a dirty word to the medical fraternity.

Jerome: The words that were used is that it’s squishy it’s soft yet I realised this was a tremendous omission, and I had never been trained to understand hope is and how to distinguish between true hope and false hope.

Devi: So what is the difference between True Hope and False Hope?
Jerome: True Hope is what I call clear eyed it sees reality and optimism says oh everything is going to be great, well as adults things don’t always turn out for the best but True hope is different it says I know what I am facing but I am going to work with my doctor to find a path to a better future.

Link: But hope can be tested when your child is diagnosed with a life threatening disease, Arabella was just 4 years old when her mother was told she had Nephroblastoma, cancer of the kidneys.

Lizle Cronje: It felt like a movie, the doctor was talking to me but I couldn’t hear anything and then they say stuff like…you should be grateful it was Wilms tumour because the survival rate is very high but still to hear your child has cancer and the to say you should feel lucky that she has that particular cancer is quiet a bitter pill to swallow.

V/O
Nephroblastoma, also called wilms tumor, grows in the kidney’s. When Arabella was diagnosed, her kidney was four times it’s size and she was in Stage 3….
What followed was 9 months of chemotherapy.

Devi what was it like for her when she lost her hair, lost her eyebrows?
Liezle: I started combing her hair and this big bunch of hair just came out. I phoned my friend and I was crying and I was please you have to do it she is not going to let me shave it off so we shaved it off together…that’s how we did it. I told her it would be fun and it was.

Devi: It’s very easy to fall into those dark spaces, how did you keep so positive?
I didn’t focus on it, this is just life this is our new normal you have to be strong for her because if I broke down crying the whole time she wouldn’t have been able or just have someone to look at and say I will be ok.

Lizle: This year is quiet big because it would be 2 years’ remission.
Devi: Why was it so significant?
Liezle: That means we are going to be ok definitely.

Devi: Does believing in something make it true and I’m talking about the the whole placebo effect?
Jerome: What Placebos teach us that there is a very powerful biology to belief and expectation to see a future that is better and that actually changes the chemistry in the brain in a very powerful way and helps the body to recover. So Hope can be as powerful as a medication as a pain reliever to reduce that degree of suffering and give the person the opportunity to really engage.

Devi: But It’s not just about positive thinking positive thinking?
Jerome: No you have to be very careful, because there is this whole Mantra if you think positively you are going to be cured well you know what that means if you have a negative thought you are responsible for your own demise you can’t think positively therefore your cancer will grow first of all that’s biologically nonsense and it’s also cruel.

Link: When Lesedi Sekgolo was 13 she started suffering from severe stomach cramps her mother took her from Dr to Dr but it was only 7 months later when she was diagnosed with a rare cancer

Devi: You finished your medical aid just trying to look for answers?
Victoria: Yes, we saw more than 6/ 7 doctors.
Devi: How did you react when you got that diagnosis?
Victoria: You know part of me was relieved that finally we knew what we were dealing with and then she was admitted at Bara and they started immediately with tests

V/O
Lesedi was diagnosed with Ewings Sarcoma, a rare and difficult cancer that usually occurs around the bones …

Lesedi: I just blacked out, I did not did not know what to do or think or feel.

V/O
She went immediately into 6 aggressive cycles of chemo therapy, pre surgery.

Victoria: When they told us how intense it was it was too much too handle but for me I just said I need to be brave to be strong for her.

Lesedi: My first 2 cycles of chemo I was pretty negative I was just angry but around my third cycle of chemo I just kinda got over myself and I thought so many people go through this I but my mom would talk about me getting my hair back, going on holiday…. . my siblings at home what they are up to so that really kept me going.

Victoria She will just look at me she will just take what I say and what I believe and it gave her hope.

Jerome: I think that intuitively people know that by giving a sense of the future that the future could be positive. its not guaranteed but it can happen and by giving that sense of hope it gives strength.

V/O
At the end of March Lesedi ended her chemotherapy and radiation treatment, but there are still on going check ups and scans to monitor her recovery.

Victoria: It was the most difficult thing I have ever experienced in my life at some point I felt if it was possible I would exchange and do it for her.

Devi: Did you have a lot of hope?
Victoria: Yes I never thought about death and I never in a single day shed a tear
Devi: Not even once in the bathroom by yourself?
Victoria: Ya by myself, yes.

V/O
NGO Reach for a Dream’s mission is to fulfil the dreams of children with severe illness’s. Arabella wanted drums.

Devi: What was that moment like when she saw the drum set.
Liezle: Oh her face…so cute she was super excited.

V/O
Lesedi, passionate about cooking asked to meet television chef, Siba.

UP SOUND Suprise

Devi: What was that moment like?
I don’t know why I burst into tears. it’s just so surreal that I met at such an incredible person when Reach for a Dream made that possible its kind of like …what isn’t possible*

V/O
Reach for a Dreams, has been fulfilling dreams like Lesedi’s for 30 years, to mark this milestone they invited Jerome to come to South Africa precisely because his message of hope ties in with their whole philosophy.

Jerome: What Reach for a dream does is try to give children an opportunity to hope and what this book I hope does is to give Dr’s a sense that with all medicines they prescribe and all of the surgeries they perform hope should be part of what’s in their black bag.

Devi: Why is it important that you never lose faith?
I feel like we all have hope within us and you just need the right circumstances for it to blossom inside of you. I feel like hope keeps us going in tough times you don’t need a guarantee you just you need little spec of hope.

Devi: There must have been times when you felt completely hopeless?
Yes there were times I thought why am I doing this why am I going through all this pain, why am I putting my family through all of this if there is no guarantee that I will make it but the thought of me giving up it would just kill me knowing I gave up too early I would rather have fought at end then not fought at all.
